case_study_insert.main_stem: Thornbury Timber & Board (TTB) is a cooperative in the sustainable forestry and recycled board sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2011 by Fiona Thorn, the business supplies low-energy fibreboard to furniture makers and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. TTB plans to invest $640,000 in a low-energy board-pressing line using recycled wood fibre, financed by a $300,000 bank overdraft and $340,000 of new member share capital. It has fixed costs of $198,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.50 a unit and a selling price of $11.00, and produces 84,000 units of board a year. TTB faces two operational problems: wood-fibre waste is above target, and defects on the new press are frequent.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The pressing line produced 21,000 boards last quarter with a defect rate of 3.4%, down from 5.2% a year ago. Wood-fibre waste ran at 8.6% of input, above the 6% target. Customer complaints fell from 41 to 26 per month. Delivery to furniture makers averaged 5.5 days. A survey of 450 furniture manufacturers found that 58% would pay up to $0.45 more for low-energy recycled board, and 44% require environmental certification before placing orders. A training audit shows 11 of 38 members have not completed on-the-job training on the new press; off-the-job courses at the college cost $780 per member.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.50%, making the $300,000 bank overdraft more expensive to carry. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $12.80 to $13.59 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Recycled wood-fibre and resin input costs have risen 11.3% year-on-year, while furniture production in the region grew 1.9% over the same period.

questions.question_text: TTB plans to fund its low-energy pressing line with new member share capital rather than the $300,000 bank overdraft. Explain two advantages for TTB of using the $340,000 share capital instead of the overdraft.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The $340,000 of new member share capital does not have to be repaid and carries no interest, so TTB avoids the volatile financing cost of a $300,000 overdraft whose rate rises with the base rate to 4.50%. For a cooperative running fixed costs of $198,000 a year, that saving protects the $5.50 contribution on each board and helps absorb the 11.3% rise in fibre and resin costs without increasing the $11.00 selling price to furniture makers.

Point 2: Share capital does not require the security or daily repayment pressure of an overdraft, so the $640,000 pressing line cannot be withdrawn by a bank at short notice if member withdrawals or a dip in orders occur. It also keeps decision-making in the hands of the cooperative's members, including founder Fiona Thorn, rather than giving a lender influence over how the recycled wood fibre is sourced. With the right to share in future profits, members have a direct incentive to reduce the 8.6% wood-fibre waste and improve the 3.4% defect rate, aligning financing with the 84,000-unit output target.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to TTB's cooperative structure, costs and ownership.

questions.question_text: TTB is launching its low-energy recycled board to furniture manufacturers. Consider advertising in a woodworking trade magazine, sponsoring a furniture trade fair, or a targeted digital campaign. Which should TTB choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Woodworking trade magazine advertising: A trade magazine reaches furniture manufacturers directly and can carry the technical detail behind TTB's low-energy board and recycled wood fibre, which is relevant to the 44% who require environmental certification. It is a credible and lasting medium for a cooperative. However, a national campaign is costly for a 38-member business with a $300,000 overdraft, much of the readership lies outside TTB's regional customer base, and print cannot prove certification or demonstrate the board's quality as effectively as face-to-face contact.

Furniture trade fair sponsorship: A sponsored stand lets TTB show samples of the recycled board, explain the pressing process and hand over certification documents to the very manufacturers who buy the 21,000 boards produced last quarter. It directly answers the 44% certification requirement and builds personal relationships. The limits are cost, limited reach to those who attend, and the fact that a single event cannot generate the orders needed for 84,000 units a year on its own.

Targeted digital campaign: Paid digital ads and emails can be aimed at furniture makers and specifiers, showing the 58% premium finding and the 5.5-day delivery record with measurable responses. It is inexpensive per contact, quick to adjust if the 3.4% defect rate needs addressing, and can be targeted on the environmental credentials that 44% demand. It relies on manufacturers engaging digitally and needs sustained spend to stay visible.

Recommendation: TTB should choose sponsorship of the furniture trade fair. Certification is a stated requirement for 44% of buyers, and only a face-to-face stand can demonstrate the recycled board and hand over documents convincingly, which a magazine cannot do and a digital campaign can only partially achieve. Digital advertising should be retained as a low-cost follow-up, while the trade magazine is rejected as expensive, untargeted and unable to prove the environmental claim that matters most.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to TTB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of TTB with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of TTB with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the magazine and digital campaign are rejected.

questions.question_text: TTB has a flat organisational structure and democratic leadership, yet wood-fibre waste is 8.6% and defects are frequent. Explain two benefits for TTB of this approach in addressing those problems.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A flat structure with democratic leadership lets TTB's 38 members speak directly to founder Fiona Thorn about the pressing line, so press operators can report the causes of the 8.6% wood-fibre waste immediately rather than waiting for messages to pass through layers of management. Faster feedback helps adjust the process before waste accumulates, protecting the $5.50 contribution on each of the 84,000 units and easing the pressure on the $640,000 investment.

Point 2: Involving members in decisions gives them ownership of quality improvements, so the 11 staff still without on-the-job training can be paired with experienced colleagues to tackle the 3.4% defect rate. Higher involvement raises commitment in a cooperative where members share in profits, reducing the complaints that fell from 41 to 26 per month and supporting the 5.5-day delivery record that furniture makers depend on. Democratic discussion also pools practical ideas from across the small workforce, which a tall hierarchy would miss.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TTB's waste, defects and cooperative structure.

questions.question_text: TTB must train 11 of its 38 members on the new press. Consider on-the-job training at the mill or off-the-job courses at the college at $780 per member. Which should TTB choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching experienced members can show the 11 trainees exactly how to reduce the 8.6% wood-fibre waste and the 3.4% defect rate on TTB's own press, at no course fee, while keeping the 21,000 boards per quarter flowing. It fits the cooperative's flat structure and democratic culture, as members learn from one another. Its weaknesses are that trainers lose production time, inconsistent habits may be passed on, and no external certificate is awarded, which matters because 44% of furniture manufacturers require environmental certification.

Off-the-job training: The college course at $780 per member costs $8,580 for all 11 (11 × $780), affordable against the $640,000 pressing line, and provides structured instruction plus a recognised certificate that supports TTB's certification claims to buyers. On the other hand, 11 of 38 members are away from the mill during the course, reducing capacity, and the generic syllabus will not cover TTB's exact press settings, so some on-site follow-up would still be necessary.

Decision: TTB should combine the two but prioritise on-the-job training, adding short college modules for the certificate. On-the-job training is cheaper, specific to the press and keeps output moving while waste is a live problem; full off-the-job training alone is rejected because losing 11 members and spending $8,580 would disrupt the 84,000-unit plan and still would not solve the mill-specific causes of the defects.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to TTB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of TTB.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of TTB with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption, certification and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TTB's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $198,000 ÷ ($11.00 − $5.50) = $198,000 ÷ $5.50 = 36,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 36,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $11.00 − $5.50 = $5.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $5.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TTB's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. The 36,000-unit break-even point against actual output of 84,000 units gives a margin of safety of 48,000 units (84,000 − 36,000), showing members how much demand can fall before the pressing line loses money.
2. Contribution of $5.50 a unit allows managers to test the $0.45 premium: if all 58% of surveyed makers paid it, contribution would rise, but if the premium were not accepted the cooperative must still cover $198,000 of fixed costs at 36,000 units.
3. Break-even and contribution figures set the volume needed to justify the $640,000 pressing line and to service the $300,000 overdraft, guiding how much recycled wood fibre must be committed.
4. Unit cost data ($198,000 ÷ 84,000 units + $5.50 = $7.86 a unit) enables benchmarking across quarters, exposing the 8.6% fibre waste and 3.4% defect rate so members can target the 11.3% input-cost inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 36,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $5.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 48,000 units against 84,000-unit output; testing the $0.45 premium against $198,000 fixed costs; volume planning for the $640,000 line and $300,000 overdraft; and unit-cost benchmarking at $7.86 to cut waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TTB's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.5%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 12.5%
ROCE 2025 = 15.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit of $352,000 on revenue of $880,000 gives 352 ÷ 880 = 0.400; 2025 gross profit of $432,000 on $960,000 gives 432 ÷ 960 = 0.450. Operating profit of $110,000 ÷ $880,000 = 0.125 and $144,000 ÷ $960,000 = 0.150. Returns on capital employed of $880,000 and $960,000 are 110 ÷ 880 = 0.125 and 144 ÷ 960 = 0.150.

Evaluation: All three measures improved. The 40.0% to 45.0% rise in the first margin is notable because cost of sales stayed at $528,000 while revenue grew by $80,000, so extra sales of recycled board were achieved without higher input spending. The 12.5% to 15.0% rise in operating profitability shows the $198,000 of fixed costs was spread over more output, and the 12.5% to 15.0% return on capital shows the $640,000 programme is beginning to earn. However, interest payable doubled from $12,000 to $16,000 as the overdraft grew, and the 11.3% rise in fibre and resin costs could reverse the cost-of-sales advantage in the next year. The 8.6% waste rate also suggests further efficiency gains are available.

Conclusion: TTB's performance has improved. Unchanged cost of sales with higher revenue lifts the first two margins, and the return on a larger capital base still rises. The main risk is dearer overdraft finance and continuing input inflation, so members should watch interest and waste closely, but the 2024–2025 figures show a clear, well-based improvement.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three profitability measures for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, capital employed and interest movements and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TTB of making low-energy recycled board from recycled wood fibre.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recycled wood fibre supports the survey finding that 58% of the 450 furniture makers questioned would pay up to $0.45 more for low-energy recycled board, protecting the $5.50 contribution on each unit despite an 11.3% rise in fibre and resin costs. It also satisfies the 44% who require environmental certification, helping TTB keep the orders that sustain 84,000 units of output and the $640,000 pressing line.

Disadvantage: Recycled fibre can vary in quality, which may raise the current 3.4% defect rate and the 8.6% wood-fibre waste as the press is adjusted, pushing up the $5.50 variable cost per unit. Certification and collection of reclaimed fibre also add cost and complexity, so unless the full $0.45 premium is secured across customers, the cooperative's margins could be squeezed while the new line beds in.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TTB's survey data, costs and pressing line.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.50%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in recycled fibre and resin costs will affect TTB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.50%): The $300,000 bank overdraft is explicitly variable-rate in effect, so a 0.75 percentage point rise adds 0.0075 × $300,000 = $2,250 a year if the full overdraft is drawn. Relative to fixed costs of $198,000 this is modest, and TTB could reduce the overdraft using the $340,000 member share capital. The main wider effect is that future borrowing for the $640,000 programme becomes dearer.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $13.59 an hour): TTB employs a workforce of 38 at the mill, so wage costs rise and cannot be avoided. The insert states neither hours worked nor individual pay, so an annual wage bill cannot be honestly calculated; the defensible comparison is productivity of 84,000 units ÷ 38 members ≈ 2,210 units per member. If output per member holds, the increase is absorbable within the $5.50 contribution, but if the 3.4% defects persist, unit labour costs will climb.

Fibre and resin costs (11.3%): These are direct inputs into the board. The insert does not split the $5.50 variable cost, so only a labelled bound is possible: if the entire variable cost rose 11.3%, that adds 0.113 × $5.50 = $0.62 per board (rounded); over 84,000 units that is $52,080 a year (84,000 × $0.62). Even a partial pass-through cuts contribution from $5.50 toward roughly $4.90, and the 58% of buyers willing to pay $0.45 more can offset only part of it.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in fibre and resin costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every board, directly reduces the contribution that funds the $300,000 overdraft and the $640,000 line, and cannot be removed by a single financing decision. The interest rise is small and reducible at $2,250, while the wage effect depends on hours not supplied in the insert and can be offset by productivity, so both are lesser threats.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to TTB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on TTB's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of TTB with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
